400.title: Pauri 40, sound: anad sunahu
400.hook: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore
400.howItsDone: At the close of most Sikh services and ceremonies, the sangat sings six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth, before Ardas; many Sikhs also recite all forty pauris as part of their morning prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gur prasaad, and your line, grace gives. Today is day four hundred on this path. Thank you for walking it. And today, the last pauri of the Anand.

Some songs end by turning to face the room. The singer stops singing about something and starts singing to the people in front of her. Anand Sahib does that in its last pauri. After thirty-nine stanzas, the fortieth opens with a call: two short words and then a long one, the way you'd call across a crowded hall to get everyone's attention. You've already learned the sound of the Anand's first pauri. Today, the sound of the fortieth, the one that closes the whole song of bliss.
screen: `A SONG TURNS TO FACE THE ROOM.` → `THE LAST PAURI OPENS WITH A CALL.` → `TODAY: THE SOUND OF THE FORTIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, slowly: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore. Take it in pieces. Anad: a-NUD. Notice it's not quite anand, the word in the title of the whole song. The Gurmukhi here is written without the nasal sound, anad, a short, open word. Then sunahu: su-NA-hu, three soft syllables, and it's a call: hear. Then the long one: vaddabhaageeho. Vadd, with the tongue curled back a little for the d, then bhaa, then gee, then ho: vadd-BHAA-gee-ho. It's a word for a group of people, said as if calling across a room. Then sagal: sa-GAL, all. Manorath: ma-NO-rath. And poore: POO-re, two beats, the last one light. Put it together: anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore. Hear how it moves. Two short words like a knock on the door, a long word that opens it, and then a line that lands. Many ragis sing it to a tune that lifts on vaddabhaageeho and settles on poore. The pauri goes on for five more lines and ends, the way Guru Amar Das ends so many, with the name Nanak and a sound of its own: the unstruck music playing. That's tomorrow. For today, let the first line get into your mouth. And this is the pauri the sangat sings after the first five at the close of services, so it's a line many Sikhs have sung hundreds of times. Anad sunahu.
screen: `ANAD: A-NUD, NOT QUITE ANAND.` · `SUNAHU: SU-NA-HU, A CALL.` · `VADDABHAAGEEHO: VADD-BHAA-GEE-HO.` · `SAGAL MANORATH POORE: A LINE THAT LANDS.` · then, large: `ANAD SUNAHU.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, not perfectly, just aloud, with a pause between the pieces: anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore. Say it once more, slower, and listen to your own voice as you'd listen to someone else's; if you know the tune, hum it. Then rest in the quiet it leaves behind, and if you pray, say Waheguru once.
Vaddabhaageeho, you of great fortune. The last pauri of the Anand, sung with the first five at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies. It begins: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore.
Your line: anad sunahu. Four hundred days in, the song is still calling. Day four hundred, done.

screen: `DAY 400 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 40, MEANING: HEAR THE BLISS.`

401.title: Pauri 40, meaning: hear the bliss
401.hook: hear the song of bliss, fortunate ones; all longings are fulfilled (Anand 40)
401.howItsDone: The fortieth pauri is sung with the first five at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, and is the last pauri of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri forty, and your line, anad sunahu. Can you still say the first line? Anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore. Today, what it means.

A sticky note on the fridge, a list of things wanted. A job. A test result. A phone call from someone. A child who sleeps through the night. Cross one off and two more get added underneath. Then someone calls out across a crowded hall: listen, you lucky ones, every one of those longings is met. That's how the last pauri of the Anand begins.
screen: `A LIST OF THINGS WANTED.` → `CROSS ONE OFF, TWO MORE APPEAR.` → `LISTEN, LUCKY ONES: ALL LONGINGS MET.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Anad sunahu: hear the bliss. Vaddabhaageeho: you of great fortune. Sagal manorath poore: all longings are fulfilled. Then the pauri says how. The Supreme Lord has been found, and every anxiety is gone. Pain, sickness and suffering leave, it says, by hearing the true bani. The saints and friends are delighted, because they've come to know it through the perfect Guru. Then a line that echoes a pauri we heard nine days ago. Back in pauri twenty-four, unripe were the speakers and unripe the hearers. Here, at the end, it flips: pure are those who hear, holy are those who speak, and the True Guru fills everything. The Anand closes with Nanak's prayer, at the Guru's feet, and a sound: the unstruck music, anahad, playing on and on, like trumpets nobody is blowing. So what does every longing met mean? Not that the list gets checked off. The pauri is sung by people who still have bills, illnesses and phone calls that don't come. The pauri says the longings are fulfilled because the One they were all reaching for has been found. The list was a long way of wanting one thing. Some Sikhs hear in this why the Anand is sung at the close of every gathering: whatever the occasion was about, the song ends where all the longings end. Every longing met.
screen: `HEAR THE BLISS, YOU FORTUNATE ONES.` · `THE LORD FOUND, EVERY ANXIETY GONE.` · `PURE ARE THE HEARERS, HOLY THE SPEAKERS.` · `THE UNSTRUCK MUSIC PLAYS ON.` · then, large: `EVERY LONGING MET.`

segments.voice: If you can find a recording of the six pauris, play the last one, from anad sunahu to the end, and let it pass through you; if not, sit with its first line. Bring one longing from your list to mind and set it gently beside the line, not to cancel it, just to see it in that light. Then breathe.
Manorath, a longing. The last pauri of the Anand: hear the bliss, fortunate ones, all manorath are fulfilled; pure are the hearers, holy the speakers; the unstruck music plays.
Your line: every longing met. The list may stay on the fridge; the song is sung anyway. Until tomorrow.

402.title: At every ceremony
402.hook: births, weddings, deaths and every service end with the six pauris and Ardas
402.howItsDone: Sikh services and ceremonies, including the Anand Karaj wedding, the naming of a child and the bhog after a death, close with six pauris of the Anand, Ardas said standing, and the sharing of karah prashad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manorath, a longing, and your line, every longing met. Today, where those six pauris actually get sung.

Notice how things end. A phone call trails off: okay, so, yeah, anyway, bye. A meeting ends when someone has to be somewhere else. A party ends when the last guest finds their coat. Plenty of endings just happen. In a Sikh community, the big days of a life end in a way that's been decided in advance, and it's the same way every time, whether the day was a wedding or a funeral.
screen: `OKAY, SO, YEAH, ANYWAY, BYE.` → `PLENTY OF ENDINGS JUST HAPPEN.` → `THESE ENDINGS ARE CHOSEN, EVERY TIME.`

segments.voice: Go to a Sikh wedding. The couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib four times while the four laavan are sung. Then the sangat sings six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth, and everyone stands for Ardas. The ceremony itself is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss, and in 1909 the British government in India passed an Anand Marriage Act recognizing it. Go to a naming. The Guru Granth Sahib is opened, a name is chosen from the first letter of the hymn it opens to, and again, the six pauris and Ardas. Go to an ordinary Sunday program, with an hour of kirtan and a talk. It ends the same way. And go, if you ever have to, to the bhog that closes the reading of the Guru Granth Sahib after someone has died. The six pauris are there too. Tradition says Guru Amar Das composed the Anand around the birth of a grandson, who was named Anand. So it began at a birth, and now it's sung at deaths too. That's the striking part. Singing a song of bliss at a funeral isn't pretending nothing hurts. Sikh teaching speaks of hukam, the order of the One, and Sikhs who sing the six pauris at a death speak of it as accepting that order with trust, even through tears. Whatever the day held, joy or grief, it's handed back the same way: bliss sung together, and then Ardas, standing. End in bliss.
screen: `A WEDDING: LAAVAN, THEN THE SIX PAURIS.` · `A NAMING, A SUNDAY: THE SAME ENDING.` · `EVEN AFTER A DEATH, THE ANAND.` · `JOY OR GRIEF, HANDED BACK THE SAME WAY.` · then, large: `END IN BLISS.`

segments.voice: Think back over yesterday's endings: your conversations, your meals, the last thing before sleep. Without judging any of it, notice whether each ending happened to you or was chosen. Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. Sikh weddings, namings, Sunday services and the bhog after a death all end the same way: six pauris of the Anand, then Ardas.
Your line: end in bliss. Joy or grief, the last song is the same. That's day four hundred two.

403.title: Anand at dusk
403.hook: the six pauris also sit inside the evening Rehras
403.howItsDone: Many Sikhs add the full Anand Sahib to their morning banis, and the evening Rehras Sahib includes its six pauris, the first five and the fortieth, before Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Karaj, and your line, end in bliss. Today, the same six pauris, not at a ceremony, but at the end of an ordinary day.

Play a song you love at seven in the morning, on the way to work, coffee in hand. Then play the same song at seven in the evening, shoes off, lights low. It's the same recording, note for note. But it isn't the same song. In the morning it pushes you out the door. In the evening it brings you home. A Sikh who keeps the daily prayers meets the Anand twice a day, in two different lights.
screen: `ONE SONG AT 7 A.M.` → `THE SAME SONG AT 7 P.M.` → `THE ANAND, TWICE A DAY.`

segments.voice: In the morning, the Rehat Maryada names the Japji, Jaap Sahib and the savaiyas, and many Sikhs add the whole Anand, all forty pauris, to those morning banis. That's the full meal. Then evening comes, and with it Rehras, the evening prayer, which we'll walk through line by line starting in two days. Near its end, Rehras carries the same six pauris you now know: the first five, and the fortieth. So the Anand frames the day. It's there at the start, in full, and it returns at dusk, shorter, like a taste of the morning's meal. Think about what the first line sounds like at each end. Anand bhaiaa meree maae: joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru. In the morning, that line goes out into the day ahead, before anything has gone right or wrong. At dusk, the day has happened. The bus was late. Someone was unkind. Something good came out of nowhere. And still the same words come: joy has come, mother. Not because the day was perfect. The line says where the joy comes from: I have found the True Guru. Not from the day. That's why it can be sung at both ends. Some families sing the evening pauris together, standing in a kitchen, or sitting on the floor of a front room with the lamps just lit. Some say them alone on a train home. The words don't change. The light does. Dusk, with joy.
screen: `MORNING: ALL FORTY PAURIS.` · `DUSK: THE SIX PAURIS INSIDE REHRAS.` · `THE SAME FIRST LINE AT BOTH ENDS.` · `THE JOY: FROM THE GURU, NOT THE DAY.` · then, large: `DUSK, WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Look at the light outside, or if it isn't evening yet, picture the sky going orange. Softly say or hum the first line two or three times, anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa, joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru, and let your whole day so far, the good and the bad, stand behind the words.
Anand bhaiaa, joy has come. The six pauris of the Anand return inside Rehras, the evening prayer, so the song of bliss frames the Sikh day at both ends.
Your line: dusk, with joy. The same words, whatever kind of day it was. Rest easy tonight.

404.title: Anand close
404.hook: forty pauris of joy that is steady, not giddy
404.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the full Anand Sahib each morning and its six pauris in the evening Rehras and at the close of every service and ceremony, and they often describe its joy as sahaj: steady, poised and not dependent on circumstance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anand bhaiaa, and your line, dusk, with joy. Today we close the Anand, after twenty-five days inside it.

Diwali night in a Punjabi neighborhood. Fireworks go up, crack open, flood the sky with color, and in two seconds they're gone, leaving smoke and a ringing in the ears. Below them, on a windowsill, a small clay lamp burns. Nobody films the lamp. But it's still burning at midnight, long after the last rocket. Both are a kind of joy. Only one of them lasts the night. For forty pauris, the Anand has been singing about the second kind.
screen: `FIREWORKS: TWO SECONDS OF COLOR.` → `A CLAY LAMP ON THE SILL.` → `STILL BURNING AT MIDNIGHT.`

segments.voice: Look back at where we've walked. The Anand opened with joy found, and a word for how it was found: sahaj, easily, with poise. Then: man meriaa; what is there that isn't in Your house; the true Name my support. Giaan anjan: everyone talks of bliss, but it's known through the Guru. It's given, not grabbed, and chaturaaee never found it. Sahsaa: the Word clears doubt. Khanniahu tikhee: the devotees' way is sharper than a sword. The treasure is within. Without the True Guru, words are unripe. Then the body, the eyes and the ears, each told the Lord's light is in them, and the breath played like music in the cave of the body. Gur prasaad: grace gives the Word. And the last pauri: hear the bliss, every longing met, the unstruck music playing on. Then we followed the six pauris out into life: weddings, namings, Sundays, the bhog after a death, and dusk at the end of an ordinary day. So what kind of joy is this? Not giddy. It doesn't depend on the day going well, which is why it can be sung at a funeral. Sahaj is a steadiness, a balance, the lamp rather than the firework. Guru Amar Das wrote a song of bliss that a person could sing in a hospital corridor and mean it. That's the joy the Anand is about: steady, because it rests on the One, not on what happens next. Steady joy.
screen: `SAHAJ: JOY FOUND WITH EASE AND POISE.` · `GIVEN, NOT GRABBED; THE TREASURE WITHIN.` · `BODY, EYES, EARS, BREATH: LIGHT IN ALL.` · `SUNG AT EVERY CEREMONY, AT BOTH ENDS.` · then, large: `STEADY JOY.`

405.title: Provisions for the road
405.hook: Rehras is said as work ends, like provisions for the night's journey
405.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib in the evening as the day's work ends, at home or in the gurdwara, often followed by Ardas; the Rehat Maryada lists its contents as nine shabads, the Benti Chaupai, a savaiya and dohra, six pauris of the Anand, the Mundavani and a slok.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, and your line, steady joy. Today a new stretch of the path begins: the evening prayer.

Late afternoon at a truck stop on the Grand Trunk Road. A driver is getting ready for the night run to Delhi. He fills a steel tiffin with rotis and dal, tops up a bottle of water, checks the tires, wipes the windshield. Nobody would set out on a long dark road without packing first. The night is coming whether he's ready or not, so he gets ready. Sikhs have a prayer for exactly this moment of the day.
screen: `A TRUCK STOP, LATE AFTERNOON.` → `A TIFFIN PACKED FOR THE NIGHT RUN.` → `NOBODY SETS OUT WITHOUT PACKING.`

segments.voice: The evening prayer is called Rehras. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, places it in the evening, after sunset. For many, that's when the day's work is done. The name is often explained from two old words: rah, the road or the way, and raas, the goods or capital a traveler carries. Provisions for the road. Some teachers also hear in it a humble petition, the request of someone setting out. Scholars discuss the exact roots, but the picture Sikhs give is clear: the day is a journey, night is the next stretch of it, and Rehras is what you pack. What's in the tiffin? In the standard Rehat Maryada order, it begins with nine shabads from the opening pages of the Guru Granth Sahib. Five are grouped under the heading So Dar, the door, and four under So Purakh, that Being. Then come the Benti Chaupai of Guru Gobind Singh, a short savaiya and a dohra, the six pauris of the Anand you've just learned, and two closing passages that end the Guru Granth Sahib itself, the Mundavani and a slok. Some Sikh traditions recite a longer form, with more hymns added. Then, in many homes, Ardas. Over the next two weeks we'll unpack it, one piece a day. For now, just notice the shape of the Sikh day. Morning prayers before the work starts. Rehras as the work ends. Provisions for the road.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehras, provisions for the road, and your line, check the tiffin. Today, the first thing in the tiffin, and you've met it before.

You come home in the evening and stop at your own front door, keys in hand. You've walked through it a thousand times. But tonight you notice it: the scuff at the bottom, the light from inside showing round the edges, the sound of someone cooking. The same door you left by this morning looks different coming home. Rehras opens with a door, and it's one the Japji already showed us at the start of the day.
screen: `KEYS IN HAND AT YOUR OWN DOOR.` → `THE SAME DOOR, A DIFFERENT LIGHT.` → `REHRAS OPENS WITH A DOOR.`

segments.voice: The first shabad of Rehras, by Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, opens with a question. So dar keha, so ghar keha: what is that door, what is that house, where You sit and take care of all? Almost the same hymn is pauri twenty-seven of the Japji, the morning prayer. The Guru Granth Sahib carries it more than once, and Sikhs who keep the daily banis sing it at both ends of the day. At dawn, inside the Japji. At dusk, as the first thing in Rehras. Then the shabad answers its own question, not with an address but with a crowd. Countless instruments play at that door, it says in paraphrase, and countless musicians. Wind, water and fire sing. The gods of the old stories sing, and the record keepers of the dead, and the scholars, the warriors, the saints. Whole worlds and galaxies sing. Those who please You sing, Guru Nanak says, steeped in love, and there are more than anyone could think of. And it closes on who sits at that door: the True One, who is and always will be, who made everything, who needs no one's orders, the King above kings. Nanak remains within His will. So Rehras doesn't begin by asking for anything. It begins by standing at the door at dusk and hearing that everything is already singing there. The door, again, at the other end of the day.
